notes.meaning: David starts by praising God, his Rock, the one who keeps him safe. David grew up as a shepherd, used to a staff and a harp. God made him into a brave and skilled warrior. So David gives God the credit for his fighting skill, not himself. The "hands" and "fingers" may point to using a sword, a sling, or a bow.

David piles up names for God: his steadfast love, his fortress, his safe tower, his rescuer, his shield. "Steadfast love" means God's faithful mercy, and every other good thing flows from it. David also thanks God for making the people willing to accept him as king. He knew his kingdom was at peace because of God's grace, not his own power. Matthew Henry sees this as a picture of people being won over to follow Jesus.

After praising God's greatness, David is amazed that God pays any attention to people at all. Humans are small and weak, yet God knows them and cares for them. The verse echoes Psalm 8:4. Praising God rightly means admitting we don't deserve His kindness. He gives it freely.

Human life is like a puff of breath. It is like a shadow that slides past and is gone. Spurgeon notes that the wording sounds like "Adam is like Abel," and Abel's name means "breath." David counts himself among these frail people. That makes God's care for him all the more wonderful.

David asks God to come down from heaven and act for him. The smoking mountains recall Mount Sinai, which smoked when God came down to give His law. It is a poetic picture of God coming to rescue His people. The "mountains" may also stand for proud, powerful enemies, which God needs only to touch. Spurgeon adds that God came down most fully when Jesus was born in Bethlehem.

David pictures lightning as God's arrows, and these arrows never miss. He asks God to scatter his enemies with them. Such vivid language shows his faith that nothing in the world can stop God's power.

"Deep waters" is a picture of danger that is about to swallow David up. God's time to help is when His people are sinking and every other help has failed. The "foreigners" may be enemy nations like the Philistines. They may also be Israelites who acted like strangers to God. Their mouths tell lies. Their "right hand," raised to swear an oath or shaken to seal a deal, cannot be trusted, because they break their promises.

New help from God calls for a new song of thanks. David will even praise God ahead of time for help He has promised. He will use his best harp, because nothing is too good for God. Even kings with armies cannot save themselves; God is the one who keeps them safe. David proudly calls himself God's "servant." Matthew Henry adds that this also points to Jesus, the Son of David, whom God brought through to victory.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read the new song as the song of grace in the New Testament. He took the ten strings as the Ten Commandments, which love fulfils.

notes.meaning: David repeats his prayer from verses 7-8, like a chorus. His enemies were still lying and still breaking their word. Saying the prayer again shows how urgent his need was and how much he trusted God to rescue him.

David now looks past the battle to the good of his whole people. He prays that their sons will be like healthy young trees growing tall and strong. He prays that their daughters will be like carved corner stones, both strong and beautiful. Corner stones hold a building together, and daughters often join families together. Raising children well is one of God's greatest gifts.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient Greek and Latin translations read "whose sons are like plants." On that reading, Augustine took verses 12-14 as a picture of the enemies' earthly wealth. He taught that believers should not envy it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 12-15 were first part of a different song and were later added to this psalm. Others, like Spurgeon, see the psalm as one whole poem by David.

notes.meaning: David pictures barns full of every kind of food and flocks growing into the tens of thousands. "Fields" here means open pastures where sheep give birth. Plenty is a gift to be used well. It should make us thankful to God, generous to friends, and kind to the poor.

Strong oxen will carry heavy loads from a rich harvest. No enemy will break through the city walls, and no one will be dragged off as a prisoner. There will be no cries of sorrow in the streets. Even small blessings like healthy cattle come from God's kindness.

A people with such blessings is truly blessed. Then the psalm climbs higher: the people whose God is the LORD are happier still. Knowing God as your own is far better than all earthly riches. Even when God does not give every earthly blessing, He gives His people something better.
